newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden PM says fundamentals should help crown firm.
newsitem.headline: Sweden PM says fundamentals should help crown firm.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said in a radio interview on Saturday that the crown should strengthen as fundamentals are so strong.
Persson also said he thought macro-economic fundamentals would bring bond yields lower.
While Swedish bond yields fell sharply in 1996, recent volatility have made them rise and the crown has softened about five percent since October last year.
"We are entering a peculiar economic situation in Sweden with both a large current account surplus ... and a surplus in public finances," Persson said.
"So the crown should strengthen, it should move in the other direction, and in turn this should pull short interest rates downwards... Fundamentals are there."
"I would also dare to guess that we...will see a continued interest rate fall in Sweden, in reference to fundamentals."
Persson said the recent market situation with climbing bond yields and a weaker crown could be described as "dents" in the positive long-term curve.
"We have previously been exposed to this kind of attacks. It happened one year ago and it happened two years ago," he said.
Analysts attribute recent market volatility to worries about whether Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) will start as planned on January 1, 1999.
When players doubt EMU plans, they flee from other European currencies to the mark, which is seen stronger on its own than as a part of the monetary union.
Market players also worry that Persson and his minority Social Democratic government could start spending money ahead of general elections in September 1998, in an effort to regain voter support.
Persson has promised to spend 10 billion crowns of an expected 1998 budget surplus on the public sector and he has indicated that Social Democrats will start recognising his party again.

Traditionally, Social Democrats favour a large public sector and generous social benefits, but since taking power in 1994 the government has implemented tough budget cutbacks to bring battered state finances in order.
With cuts in social benefits and a for Sweden very high unemployment, 8.8 percent in February, polls show Social Democratic voter support falling.

But Persson, who moved from the Finance Minister post to become Prime Minister a year ago, reiterated that he thought the government would be able to keep its promise to cut open unemployment to four percent by the year 2000.
Considering that a general economic uppick is expected to boost employment, he said the government's task consisted of creating an additional 70,000-80,000 jobs over three years.
"I don't think that task is impossible," he said.
He opened for shorter work hours as a possible way to help bring unemployment down.
"You can think about what would happen in an economy ... if growth is created without more jobs," he said.
"In such a situation, I think that more and more people would like to start discussing shorter work hours and then you have to be open for that."
-- Birgitta Forsberg, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006
